messages.subject: Inconsistent timing for HMC runs
parts:
I noticed when using Stan to run HMC that there was a lot of variation in the sampling time of my models. I ran a quick test of this, taking the 8-schools model and running it across a int_time of 1 to 20 and a 20 different seeds. As it turns out, the timings for the warmup period are very consistent and scale with int_time as expected. However, the sampling time was indeed very variable. Further, I ran NUTS with the same seeds and took the mean of the n_leapfrog__ for the warmup and sampling periods and that doesn't match the same pattern as HMC. Below is some quick simulation code.



From what I understand of these algorithms, particularly HMC, the core computational costs are the leapfrog algorithm, and even if the algorithm rejected every proposal it should take the same time as one that accepted every proposal.

This raises several questions:
  1. Why would the sampling period for HMC be variable when the warmup was not (both were the same number of iterations)?
  2. Shouldn't HMC be very consistent and scale directly with int_time?
  3. Shouldn't the NUTS algorithm take the same time as HMC given the same number of total leapfrog steps?
  4. Shouldn't the timing be independent of the tuning parameters, given total leapfrog steps? 
  5. Am I missing something obvious here?
System Info:
R version 3.2.2 (2015-08-14)
Platform: x86_64-w64-mingw32/x64 (64-bit)
Running under: Windows 8 x64 (build 9200)
Rstan=2.8.2
Rtools gcc= 4.6.3

Here's code to reproduce this test, using the 8schools.stan model.
## Speed tests for Stan algorithms. HMC should scale linearly with int_time
## and NUTS should be similar for average n_leapfrog__ for the warmup and
## sampling period.
seeds <- 1:20
int_time <- seq(1,20, by=2)
Nsim <- 5000
schools_dat <- list(J=8, y=c(28,8,-3,7,-1,1,18,12), sigma=c(15,10,16,11,9,11,10,18))
fit <- stan(file='schools/schools.stan', data=schools_dat, iter=10,
                chains=1, seed=seed, algorithm='HMC', control=list(int_time=1))
speed.hmc <-
  ldply(seeds, function(seed){
          fit.hmc <- ldply(int_time, function(L){
                    fit <- stan(fit=fit, data=schools_dat, iter=Nsim,
                                chains=1, seed=seed, algorithm='HMC', control=list(int_time=L))
                    data.frame(L=L, seed=seed, rstan::get_elapsed_time(fit))
                    })})
speed.nuts <-
  ldply(seeds, function(seed){
          fit <- stan(fit=fit, data=schools_dat, iter=Nsim,
                      chains=1, seed=seed, algorithm='NUTS')
          temp <- data.frame(get_sampler_params(fit))
          data.frame(warmup.nleap=mean(temp[(1:Nsim/2), 'n_leapfrog__']),
                          sample.nleap=mean(temp[-(1:Nsim/2),'n_leapfrog__']),
                          get_elapsed_time(fit), seed=seed)})
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(warmup~L, data=speed.hmc, ylab="Time", xlab="Steps", main='Warmup',
     ylim=c(0, max(speed.hmc$sample)))
points(warmup~warmup.nleap, data=speed.nuts, col='red', pch=2)
plot(sample~L, data=speed.hmc, ylab="Time", xlab="Steps", main='Sample',
     ylim=c(0, max(speed.hmc$sample)))
points(sample~sample.nleap, data=speed.nuts, col='red', pch=2)
legend('topleft', legend=c("HMC", "NUTS"), col=c('black', 'red'), pch=c(1,2))

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Inconsistent timing for HMC runs
parts:
Firstly, when including figures please make sure that they are large enough to at least
read the axis labels easily enough.

Secondly, let me be a bit pedantic regarding names.  Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)
is a very generic way of generating high-performance Markov chains.  NUTS is one
_implementation_ of HMC.  As is _static HMC_, which uses a constant integration 
time and takes the final point as a proposal.  In your comparisons you are comparing
static HMC with NUTS.

Thirdly, integration time is not equal to the number of leapfrog steps.  Rather integration
time is the product of the integrator step size and total number of leapfrog steps, so
n_leapfrog = int_time / epsilon.  Also, the mean n_leapfrog in NUTS isn’t particularly
helpful due to the typical skewness of the distribution.

Finally, your expectations are almost correct _conditioned on all other tuning parameters 
being the same_.  In particular, the integrator step size and mass matrix can make huge
differences in the computational cost of a transition.  This is important because the
adaptation we do in warmup learns these other tuning parameters, and varying adaptation
leads to varying performance.  

Long story short, to do a proper comparison you’ll want to turn adaptation off to ensure
the same tuning parameters and make sure to compare the number of leapfrog steps
and not the integration time.
1. Why would the sampling period for HMC be variable when the warmup was not (both were the same number of iterations)?

Because of adaptation in warmup.  See the manual for a discussion of our windowed
adaptation procedure.  In particular, with iter=10 you have only 5 warmup iterations
which will update the mass matrix only once, after the fifth iteration.  If you use a
much more reasonable warmup then you’ll start to see variation in warmup timings,
too.
1. Shouldn't HMC be very consistent and scale directly with int_time?

Practical implementations of HMC use numerical integrators, which imply that the
algorithms should scales with the number of leapfrog steps, not integration time
directly.
1. Shouldn't the NUTS algorithm take the same time as HMC given the same number of total leapfrog steps?

Transition by transition, yes, if you ignore algorithmic overhead.  But that doesn’t
mean that they will when you average over chains set to different tunings.
1. Shouldn't the timing be independent of the tuning parameters, given total leapfrog steps?

If you could set the total leapfrog steps then yes.  But you can’t do that in any of
our samplers right now.

Those are two reparameterizations of the same problem, one is
really not different from the other in practice.  The computational
consequence is on how well-chosen the mass matrix is with
respect to the target distribution.

Stan estimates an optimal mass matrix (really Euclidean metric)
in windows during warmup, updating the mass matrix to the best
current estimate at the end of each window.
I think it would be valuable for the user to be able to specify the number of steps opposed to the integration time.

steps depends on the step size — in other words only the
integration time and step size can be optimized independently
of each other.  People keep making this mistake in the literature
and it causes no end of confusion that we (often I) have to clean
up.

It took a lot of cluster computing to generate those figures.

with the big change targeted for Stan 3. That should also allow
more control over specifying mass matrices; but we think that's

be able to put in much more algorithm description before referring
people to the code (though that's the best we have now and will
always be the final arbiter of what Stan actually does in practice).

to be one step and get Langevin?

parts: Michael --- isn't Langevin just 1 step of HMC?

Yup.  Well, the “Metropolis-Adjusted Langevin Algorithm”
is if you really want to be pedantic.

And if so, for a fixed step size (discretization interval),
couldn't we just fix integration time to be one step and get Langevin?

If the step size is fixed then you could do int_time = epsilon.
Or, noting that the minimum number of leapfrog steps is 1,
you could also set int_time to something really small and
for any reasonable adapted step size you’d still get Langevin.

But just because you _could_ do it doesn’t mean that you should….

It is in CmdStan, which distinguishes between algorithm (HMC) and 
engine (static or NUTS).  The conventions used in RStan (and then
PyStan) were not proposed by the entire team.  This will hopefully
be remedied in the refactor.

It seems most other software programs with HMC (e.g., ADMB), as well as the papers describing it, you specify step size and number of steps. I think it might be worth explaining this in the adaptation section of the manual. The term int_time isn't used at all there, not really described in the help files in Rstan.

And just about every implementation of HMC outside of Stan is
just a reimplementation of code in the NUTS paper or Stan itself.
Integration time is more natural, especially when trying to optimize
the various free parameters in HMC.  Trying to optimize step size
and number of leapfrog steps introduces all kinds of problems, as
evident in many, many papers.

Again, the inconsistencies between the interfaces is a known problem
and we are working to improve that.

Finally, your expectations are almost correct _conditioned on all other tuning parameters 
being the same_.  In particular, the integrator step size and mass matrix can make huge
differences in the computational cost of a transition.  This is important because the
adaptation we do in warmup learns these other tuning parameters, and varying adaptation
leads to varying performance.  

Neal (2011) describes two ways of using the mass matrix:  a Chloesky decomposition of parameter space or using it in the kinetic energy function. The first seems to be more population. Does Stan use the mass matrix to do a Cholesky decomposition? Is that why there are such computational differences depending on tuning parameters? Are the differences only in unit vs. diagonal vs. dense matrices, or can there also be differences between different dense matrices (e.g. taking advantage of sparseness)?

Those are two reparameterizations of the same problem, one is
really not different from the other in practice.  The computational
consequence is on how well-chosen the mass matrix is with
respect to the target distribution.

Stan estimates an optimal mass matrix (really Euclidean metric)
in windows during warmup, updating the mass matrix to the best
current estimate at the end of each window.

I think it would be valuable for the user to be able to specify the number of steps opposed to the integration time.

No, it would not.  The optimal value of the number of leapfrog
steps depends on the step size — in other words only the
integration time and step size can be optimized independently
of each other.  People keep making this mistake in the literature
and it causes no end of confusion that we (often I) have to clean
up.

For instance Langevin sampling can't be done directly in Stan (if I understand correctly). I could see that being potentially useful for some people in some models.

There is no reason for ever using Langevin over HMC — if there
were I can assure you that it would be in Stan.  We’re not just
implementing algorithms here, we’re also the ones actively
researching them.

What was the reasoning behind specifying integration time instead?

See above.

Also, the calculation from n_step=int_time/stepsize isn't integer.. is this value rounded up?

It rounds per the implementation of C++,
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/develop/src/stan/mcmc/hmc/static/base_static_hmc.hpp


I'm new to Stan but really like it so far and appreciate all the development that has gone into it. I think it may be helpful to the user base to have a more thorough explanation of the adaptation procedure that is going on internally. This will be particularly true for users who come from other software platforms or have coded it themselves on specific problems. For example I couldn't find the default behavior of argument metric, or how to pass an arbitrary mass matrix.

See Section 57.2 of the manual.  This is all extensively documented, and any
confusion can be resolved by looking at the code directly.

Is it correct that this is what happens when using static HMC: (1) User gives int_time, (2) a 'reasonable' stepsize is found and from this an approximate number of leapfrog steps (L), (3) the warmup procedure begins and stepsize is updated (and hence L) using dual averaging. (4) Continue with sampling.

The initial step size in (2) does not depend on the choice of integration time.
It uses the error from a single step.

>>
>> I was a bit too brief. ADMB was essentially written by a single person and then was recently bought and turned open source. It was/is designed for maximum likelihood estimation with MCMC capabilities tacked on (since why not?).

The reason not to implement Metropolis for users is that
you don't want to give them something that's going to return
the wrong answer.

This is why we're so worried about variational inference at the
moment and why it has a big "EXPERIMENTAL" tag on it. Even in
cases where it returns an answer, we don't undrestand the properties
of the answer (either the point estimate of the approximating density
or its variance).

There are models for which Metropolis will seem to mix OK,
non-robust autocorrelation estimators like the one in Coda
(a popular R package) will be used to assess effective sample
size and miss long-term corelations, and the user will be led
to believe they've converged and can estimate posterior
expectations when in fact their results will be wrong.
>> It's amazingly robust and fast at optimization.

Optimization's relatively well understood. At least for
convex problems.
>> If the Hessian at the mode is positive definite it will use the inverse for the RWM multivariate normal, or the mass matrix for the static HMC.

Is there a description of the algorithm somewhere?

The problem you run into with that approach is that the
mode often doesn't exist, or is not in the typical set, or the
posterior has varying curvature so that a static estimate
won't work well. We've found a diagonal variance to be more
robust and we have to compensate by taking small step sizes so
that an iterated first-order gradient can deal with the curvature.
But that introduces problems like stiff ODE solvers.

- Bob
